Let \(s=q^2+1\) be the number of spread lines. The total number of lines of \(PG(3,q)\) is

\[
\binom{4}{2}_q=(q^2+1)(q^2+q+1),
\]

so the number of vertices of \(\Gamma\) is

\[
n=(q^2+1)(q^2+q)=q(q+1)(q^2+1).
\]

Let \(A\) be the adjacency matrix of the full line-intersection graph on all projective lines, and let \(B\) be the adjacency matrix of \(\Gamma\).

A line of \(PG(3,q)\) has \(q+1\) points, and through each point there are \(q^2+q+1\) lines. Hence the full line graph has degree

\[
k=(q+1)(q^2+q)=q(q+1)^2.
\]

Every non-spread line meets exactly \(q+1\) spread lines, one through each of its points. Therefore \(\Gamma\) is regular of degree

\[
d=k-(q+1)=q^3+2q^2-1.
\]

Now form the \(s\times n\) matrix \(C\), whose rows are spread lines and whose columns are non-spread lines, with

\[
C_{\ell,L}=1 \iff \ell\cap L\neq \varnothing.
\]

Each row has sum \(k=q(q+1)^2\), each column has sum \(q+1\). For two distinct spread lines \(\ell_1,\ell_2\), the number of non-spread lines meeting both is \((q+1)^2\), since such a line is determined by a choice of one point on each spread line. Thus

\[
CC^{T}=q(q+1)^2 I+(q+1)^2(J-I)
=(q+1)^2\bigl((q-1)I+J\bigr).
\]

So \(C\) has full row rank \(q^2+1\). On vectors \(x\perp \mathbf 1\) in the spread-line space,

\[
CC^{T}x=(q-1)(q+1)^2x.
\]

We next compute how \(B\) acts on \(\operatorname{im} C^T\). Fix a spread line \(\ell\) and a non-spread line \(L\). The number of non-spread lines meeting both \(\ell\) and \(L\), excluding \(L\), is

\[
2q^2+q-1
\]

if \(L\) meets \(\ell\), and is

\[
(q+1)^2
\]

if \(L\) is skew to \(\ell\). Hence

\[
CB=(q+1)^2J+\bigl(2q^2+q-1-(q+1)^2\bigr)C
=(q+1)^2J+(q^2-q-2)C.
\]

Therefore, for \(x\perp \mathbf 1\),

\[
B(C^Tx)=(q^2-q-2)C^Tx.
\]

This gives eigenvalue

\[
\beta=q^2-q-2=(q+1)(q-2)
\]

with multiplicity \(q^2\).

The remaining space is \(\ker C\), of dimension

\[
n-(q^2+1)=(q^2+1)(q^2+q-1).
\]

The full line-intersection graph has spectrum obtained from point-line incidence. If \(M\) is the point-line incidence matrix, then

\[
A=M^TM-(q+1)I.
\]

Also

\[
MM^T=q(q+1)I+J,
\]

so the nontrivial eigenvalues of \(A\) are

\[
q^2-1,\qquad -(q+1).
\]

Since \(\ker C\) is \(B\)-invariant, the remaining eigenvalues of \(B\) are among these two. Let their multiplicities be \(a,b\). We already have the eigenvalue \(d\) once and \(\beta\) with multiplicity \(q^2\), so

\[
a+b=n-1-q^2=q^4+q^3+q-1.
\]

Using \(\operatorname{tr}B=0\),

\[
d+q^2\beta+a(q^2-1)-b(q+1)=0.
\]

Solving gives

\[
a=q(q^2+1),\qquad b=q^4-1.
\]

Thus the adjacency spectrum of \(\Gamma\) is

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{eigenvalue} & \text{multiplicity}\\
\hline
d=q^3+2q^2-1 & 1\\
q^2-q-2 & q^2\\
q^2-1 & q(q^2+1)\\
-(q+1) & q^4-1
\end{array}
\]

Since \(\Gamma\) is \(d\)-regular, its Laplacian eigenvalues are \(d-\lambda\). By Kirchhoff’s matrix-tree theorem,

\[
\tau(\Gamma)=\frac1n
\bigl(d-(q^2-q-2)\bigr)^{q^2}
\bigl(d-(q^2-1)\bigr)^{q(q^2+1)}
\bigl(d+q+1\bigr)^{q^4-1}.
\]

Now

\[
d-(q^2-q-2)=q^3+q^2+q+1=(q+1)(q^2+1),
\]

\[
d-(q^2-1)=q^3+q^2=q^2(q+1),
\]

and

\[
d+q+1=q(q+1)^2.
\]

Since \(n=q(q+1)(q^2+1)\), the number of spanning trees is

\[
\boxed{
q^{q^4+2q^3+2q-2}
(q+1)^{2q^4+q^3+q^2+q-3}
(q^2+1)^{q^2-1}
}.
\]
